name: Park Slope Food Coop
who: Member-labor food co-op with 16,700+ members and one storefront, open since 1973.
why: Defined the American working-co-op model — every member works a shift, and it still runs on that rule alone.

name: Berkeley Bowl
who: Independent produce-and-grocery market, two locations, open since 1977.
why: The produce range and sourcing set the reference point other independents get measured against.

name: Rainbow Grocery Cooperative
who: Worker-owned natural foods co-op since 1975, no outside investors, heavy bulk and vegetarian focus.
why: One of the last surviving worker-owned grocery co-ops and a fixture of San Francisco food culture.

name: PCC Community Markets
who: Nation's largest consumer-owned food co-op, 117,000+ members, 16 certified-organic stores since 1953.
why: Started as a 15-family buying club and scaled into the biggest co-op grocery network in the country.

name: Wheatsville Food Co-op
who: Austin's oldest food co-op, two full-service member-owned grocery stores, open since 1976.
why: A longtime local institution running a full grocery format on co-op ownership.

name: Hanover Co-op Food Stores
who: Consumer co-op founded 1936 as a 17-family buying club; now three stores, a market, and a service center.
why: Among the oldest surviving consumer co-ops in the country, still owned by the community that started it.

name: Willy Street Co-op
who: Community-owned natural foods co-op with three Madison locations, founded 1972.
why: A Midwest anchor co-op with a following bigger than its store count suggests.

name: Ocean Beach People's Food Co-op
who: San Diego's only grocery co-op, founded 1971 as a buying club, fully certified-organic produce department.
why: The city's sole surviving food co-op, still tracing straight back to a 1971 buying club.

name: The Wedge Community Co-op
who: Founded 1974 in a Minneapolis basement; now one of the largest single-site natural foods co-ops in the US.
why: A founding-era Twin Cities co-op that helped seed the Midwest natural-foods movement.

name: Seward Community Co-op
who: Member-owned natural foods co-op with two Minneapolis stores, sister institution to the Wedge.
why: A long-running Twin Cities co-op built on volunteer culture and community programming.

name: Central Co-op
who: Community-owned natural foods co-op on Capitol Hill, plus a Tacoma location, known for social-justice-minded sourcing.
why: A values-driven co-op distinct from PCC, with a strong Capitol Hill identity.

name: Bloomingfoods
who: Community-owned co-op grocer since 1976 with multiple Bloomington, Indiana locations.
why: A durable small-city co-op feeding a college town's natural-foods demand for five decades.

name: La Montanita Co-op
who: Largest food co-op in the Southwest, stores across Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Gallup, and Los Alamos plus its own distribution center.
why: A regional co-op network, not just a single store, built around New Mexico's local-food supply chain.

name: City Market, Onion River Co-op
who: Burlington's community-owned grocery co-op, successor to the original Onion River Co-op buying club.
why: Vermont's flagship food co-op, anchoring one of the most co-op-dense food scenes in the country.

name: Sevananda Natural Foods Market
who: Atlanta's only cooperative grocery, open since 1974 in Little Five Points, 4,000+ member-owners.
why: A 50-year survivor and the sole co-op grocery left standing in a major Southern city.

name: MOM's Organic Market (Rockville)
who: The original location of the MOM's Organic Market chain, founded 1987, now the DC area's largest organic grocery brand.
why: The founding store of a regional organic-grocery chain built on a strict banned-ingredients list.
